claim: Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) and osteolineage cells contribute to the hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) niche in the bone marrow of long bones.
source: Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) and osteolineage cells contribute to the hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) niche in the bone marrow of long bones.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact that provides context for the study.

claim: The developmental relationships between MSCs and osteolineage cells remain unclear.
source: However, their developmental relationships remain unclear.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Different MSC populations in the developing marrow of long bones have distinct functions.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that different MSC populations in the developing marrow of long bones have distinct functions.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Proliferative mesoderm-derived nestin− MSCs participate in fetal skeletogenesis.
source: Proliferative mesoderm-derived nestin− MSCs participate in fetal skeletogenesis and lose MSC activity soon after birth.
evidence: This finding is supported by lineage tracing experiments and functional assays shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Mesoderm-derived nestin− MSCs lose MSC activity soon after birth.
source: Proliferative mesoderm-derived nestin− MSCs participate in fetal skeletogenesis and lose MSC activity soon after birth.
evidence: This is demonstrated by CFU-F assays showing progressive loss of activity in nestin-negative cells (Figure 3H).

claim: Quiescent neural crest-derived nestin+ cells preserve MSC activity.
source: In contrast, quiescent neural crest-derived nestin+ cells preserve MSC activity, but do not generate fetal chondrocytes.
evidence: This is supported by CFU-F assays (Figure 3H) and lineage tracing experiments (Figures 2 and 4).

claim: Neural crest-derived nestin+ cells do not generate fetal chondrocytes.
source: In contrast, quiescent neural crest-derived nestin+ cells preserve MSC activity, but do not generate fetal chondrocytes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by fate mapping studies using Nes-CreERT2 and Wnt1-Cre2 mice (Figure 2).

claim: Neural crest-derived nestin+ cells differentiate into HSC niche-forming MSCs.
source: Instead, they differentiate into HSC niche-forming MSCs, helping to establish the HSC niche by secreting Cxcl12.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing high expression of HSC maintenance genes (Figure 5B) and functional studies (Figure 7).

claim: Neural crest-derived nestin+ cells help establish the HSC niche by secreting Cxcl12.
source: Instead, they differentiate into HSC niche-forming MSCs, helping to establish the HSC niche by secreting Cxcl12.
evidence: This is demonstrated by conditional deletion of Cxcl12 in nestin+ cells, which impairs HSC migration to bone marrow (Figure 7N-O).

claim: Perineural migration of neural crest-derived cells to the bone marrow requires the ErbB3 receptor.
source: Perineural migration of these cells to the bone marrow requires the ErbB3 receptor.
evidence: This is demonstrated using Erbb3-deficient mice, which show reduced bone marrow MSCs and HSCs (Figure 6).

claim: The neonatal Nestin-GFP+ Pdgfrα− cell population contains Schwann cell precursors.
source: The neonatal Nestin-GFP+ Pdgfrα− cell population also contains Schwann cell precursors, but does not comprise mature Schwann cells.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing expression of Schwann cell precursor genes (Sox10, Plp1, Erbb3, Dhh) but not mature Schwann cell genes like Gfap (Figure 5C).

claim: The neonatal Nestin-GFP+ Pdgfrα− cell population does not comprise mature Schwann cells.
source: The neonatal Nestin-GFP+ Pdgfrα− cell population also contains Schwann cell precursors, but does not comprise mature Schwann cells.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing lack of Gfap expression in this population (Figure 5C).

claim: HSC niche-forming MSCs share a common origin with sympathetic peripheral neurons and glial cells.
source: Thus, in the developing bone marrow HSC niche-forming MSCs share a common origin with sympathetic peripheral neurons and glial cells, and ontogenically distinct MSCs have non-overlapping functions in endochondrogenesis and HSC niche formation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by neural crest lineage tracing using Wnt1-Cre2 and Sox10-CreERT2 mice (Figure 4).

claim: Ontogenically distinct MSCs have non-overlapping functions in endochondrogenesis and HSC niche formation.
source: Thus, in the developing bone marrow HSC niche-forming MSCs share a common origin with sympathetic peripheral neurons and glial cells, and ontogenically distinct MSCs have non-overlapping functions in endochondrogenesis and HSC niche formation.
evidence: This is the central conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of evidence including lineage tracing, functional assays, and gene expression analysis.

claim: GFP+ cells were present in E16.5 bone marrow, associated preferentially with blood vessels infiltrating the cartilage scaffold.
source: GFP+ cells were already present in E16.5 bone marrow, associated preferentially with blood vessels infiltrating the cartilage scaffold (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This observation is supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: At E18.5 Nes-GFP+ cells were frequently associated with arterioles and sprouting endothelial cells within the osteochondral junction.
source: At E18.5 Nes-GFP+ cells were frequently associated with arterioles and sprouting endothelial cells within the osteochondral junction (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: Fetal bone marrow Nes-GFP+ cells were heterogeneous, composed of a majority of BMSCs but also including a small subset of CD31+ putative endothelial cells.
source: Fetal bone marrow Nes-GFP+ cells were heterogeneous, composed of a majority of BMSCs but also including a small subset of CD31+ putative endothelial cells that increased during the postnatal period (Figure 1D,E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: The subset of CD31+ putative endothelial cells within Nes-GFP+ cells increased during the postnatal period.
source: Fetal bone marrow Nes-GFP+ cells were heterogeneous, composed of a majority of BMSCs but also including a small subset of CD31+ putative endothelial cells that increased during the postnatal period (Figure 1D,E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry comparing E18.5 and 1-week old mice (Figure 1D-E).

claim: Compared with Nes-GFP- BMSCs, the Nes-GFP+ cell population was enriched in endogenous Nestin mRNA expression.
source: Compared with Nes-GFP- BMSCs, the Nes-GFP+ cell population was enriched in endogenous Nestin mRNA expression (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Arterioles were associated with an intense fluorescence microscopy signal, due to the presence of several concentric GFP+ cells.
source: Arterioles were associated with an intense fluorescence microscopy signal, due to the presence of several concentric GFP+ cells, including an outer layer that expressed smooth muscle actin and an inner layer of endothelial cells (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: Arterioles have an outer layer of GFP+ cells that expressed smooth muscle actin and an inner layer of endothelial cells.
source: Arterioles were associated with an intense fluorescence microscopy signal, due to the presence of several concentric GFP+ cells, including an outer layer that expressed smooth muscle actin and an inner layer of endothelial cells (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence co-staining shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Fetal bone marrow Nes-GFP+ cells were distinct from S100-expressing chondrocytes.
source: Fetal bone marrow Nes-GFP+ cells were distinct from S100-expressing chondrocytes and osteoblastic cells genetically labeled with the 2.3-kilobase proximal fragment of the α1(I)-collagen promoter (Dacquin et al., 2002) (Figure 1H–J).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 1H-J.

claim: Fetal bone marrow Nes-GFP+ cells were distinct from osteoblastic cells genetically labeled with the 2.3-kilobase proximal fragment of the α1(I)-collagen promoter.
source: Fetal bone marrow Nes-GFP+ cells were distinct from S100-expressing chondrocytes and osteoblastic cells genetically labeled with the 2.3-kilobase proximal fragment of the α1(I)-collagen promoter (Dacquin et al., 2002) (Figure 1H–J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by genetic labeling and immunofluorescence shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Nes-GFP- BMSCs showed marked proliferation in perinatal life.
source: Contrasting the marked proliferation of Nes-GFP- BMSCs in perinatal life, Nes-GFP+ cells remained mostly quiescent (Figure 1K and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell cycle analysis shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Nes-GFP+ cells remained mostly quiescent in perinatal life.
source: Contrasting the marked proliferation of Nes-GFP- BMSCs in perinatal life, Nes-GFP+ cells remained mostly quiescent (Figure 1K and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell cycle analysis showing low percentage of cells in G2/S-M phase (Figure 1K).

claim: Nes-GFP- BMSCs steadily expanded in number during the postnatal period.
source: As a result, whereas Nes-GFP- BMSCs steadily expanded, Nes-GFP+ BMSC number did not change significantly (Figure 1L).
evidence: This is shown by quantification of cell numbers over time in Figure 1L.

claim: Nes-GFP+ BMSC number did not change significantly during the postnatal period.
source: As a result, whereas Nes-GFP- BMSCs steadily expanded, Nes-GFP+ BMSC number did not change significantly (Figure 1L).
evidence: This is shown by quantification of cell numbers over time in Figure 1L.

claim: Fetal bone marrow Nes-GFP+ cells include a small subset (<10%) of endothelial cells and a large population of non-endothelial stromal cells (>90%).
source: Fetal bone marrow Nes-GFP+ cells thus include a small subset (<10%) of endothelial cells and a large population of non-endothelial stromal cells (>90%).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Unlike Nes-GFP- stromal cells, Nes-GFP+ cells proliferate slowly and do not express osteochondral protein cell markers.
source: Unlike Nes-GFP- stromal cells, Nes-GFP+ cells proliferate slowly and do not express osteochondral protein cell markers.
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle analysis (Figure 1K) and immunofluorescence staining (Figure 1H-J).

claim: Unlike osteoblast precursors derived from lateral plate mesoderm, Nes-GFP+ cells in fetal-limb bone marrow did not express highly osterix protein.
source: Unlike osteoblast precursors derived from lateral plate mesoderm, Nes-GFP+ cells in fetal-limb bone marrow did not express highly osterix protein (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining comparing Nes-Gfp and Hoxb6-CreERT2;RCE mice (Figure 2A-B).

claim: Tamoxifen administration triggers labeling of Nes-GFP+ cells and their progeny in Nes-CreERT2 mice.
source: In these mice, tamoxifen administration triggers labeling of Nes-GFP+ cells and their progeny (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-localization of GFP and Tomato signals in Figure 2C.

claim: Unlike Hoxb6-traced mesodermal derivatives, nestin+ cells did not contribute to cartilage formation during the fetal period.
source: Unlike Hoxb6-traced mesodermal derivatives, nestin+ cells did not contribute to cartilage formation during this period.
evidence: This is demonstrated by fate mapping studies shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: Nes-traced cells with a similar morphology and distribution to Nes-GFP+ cells were observed in the chondro–osseous junction.
source: In contrast, Nes-traced cells with a similar morphology and distribution to Nes-GFP+ cells were observed in the chondro–osseous junction (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is shown by fate mapping in Figure 2D'-D'' and 2F.

claim: Nes-GFP+ cells were not present inside the cartilage but were found in the innermost part of the perichondrium.
source: Similarly, Nes-GFP+ cells were not present inside the cartilage but were found in the innermost part of the perichondrium (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), a region enriched in MSCs (Maes et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2013; Zaidi and Mendez-Ferrer, 2013).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and supported by citations.

claim: The innermost part of the perichondrium is a region enriched in MSCs.
source: Similarly, Nes-GFP+ cells were not present inside the cartilage but were found in the innermost part of the perichondrium (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), a region enriched in MSCs (Maes et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2013; Zaidi and Mendez-Ferrer, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: CFU-F efficiency was nearly three times higher in Nes-GFP- cells than in Nes-GFP+ cells at E17.5.
source: CFU-F efficiency was nearly three times higher in Nes-GFP- cells than in Nes-GFP+ cells at E17.5 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CFU-F assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Non-adherent sphere formation was markedly enriched in GFP+ cells.
source: Conversely, non-adherent sphere formation was markedly enriched in GFP+ cells, whereas most spheres derived from GFP− cells rapidly attached to plastic and spontaneously differentiated into adipocytes (Figure 3B–G), suggesting that Nes-GFP- BMSCs are in a more committed state.
evidence: This is demonstrated by mesensphere assays shown in Figure 3B-G.

claim: Most spheres derived from GFP− cells rapidly attached to plastic and spontaneously differentiated into adipocytes.
source: Conversely, non-adherent sphere formation was markedly enriched in GFP+ cells, whereas most spheres derived from GFP− cells rapidly attached to plastic and spontaneously differentiated into adipocytes (Figure 3B–G), suggesting that Nes-GFP- BMSCs are in a more committed state.
evidence: This is shown by Oil Red O staining in Figure 3F-G.

claim: Nes-GFP- BMSCs are in a more committed state than Nes-GFP+ cells.
source: Conversely, non-adherent sphere formation was markedly enriched in GFP+ cells, whereas most spheres derived from GFP− cells rapidly attached to plastic and spontaneously differentiated into adipocytes (Figure 3B–G), suggesting that Nes-GFP- BMSCs are in a more committed state.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential behavior in sphere formation and spontaneous differentiation assays.

claim: Spheres formed by Nes-GFP+ bone marrow cells contained mesenchyme-like spindle-shaped GFP+ cells.
source: Spheres formed by Nes-GFP+ bone marrow cells contained mesenchyme-like spindle-shaped GFP+ cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown by microscopy images in Figure 3E.

claim: At E18.5 and during the first postnatal week, CFU-F frequency was 6-fold higher in the GFP− stromal population than in GFP+ cells.
source: At E18.5 and during the first postnatal week, CFU-F frequency was 6-fold higher in the GFP− stromal population than in GFP+ cells (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CFU-F assays shown in Figure 3H.

claim: At later postnatal stages, CFU-F activity was progressively restricted to Nes-GFP+ cells due to a sharp drop in activity in GFP− BMSCs.
source: However, at later postnatal stages, CFU-F activity was progressively restricted to Nes-GFP+ cells due to a sharp drop in activity in GFP− BMSCs (>100-fold reduction between E18.5 and P14, compared with a 0.5-fold reduction in Nes-GFP+ cells).
evidence: This is demonstrated by longitudinal CFU-F assays shown in Figure 3H.

claim: There was a >100-fold reduction in CFU-F activity in GFP− BMSCs between E18.5 and P14.
source: However, at later postnatal stages, CFU-F activity was progressively restricted to Nes-GFP+ cells due to a sharp drop in activity in GFP− BMSCs (>100-fold reduction between E18.5 and P14, compared with a 0.5-fold reduction in Nes-GFP+ cells).
evidence: This is quantified from CFU-F assays shown in Figure 3H.

claim: There was a 0.5-fold reduction in CFU-F activity in Nes-GFP+ cells between E18.5 and P14.
source: However, at later postnatal stages, CFU-F activity was progressively restricted to Nes-GFP+ cells due to a sharp drop in activity in GFP− BMSCs (>100-fold reduction between E18.5 and P14, compared with a 0.5-fold reduction in Nes-GFP+ cells).
evidence: This is quantified from CFU-F assays shown in Figure 3H.

claim: At P7, CFU-Fs derived from Nes-GFP- cells contained mostly preosteoblasts.
source: At P7, CFU-Fs derived from Nes-GFP- cells contained mostly preosteoblasts (Figure 3I–K).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CFU-OB assays and staining shown in Figure 3I-K.

claim: The expression of genes associated with chondrocyte development was higher in Nes-GFP- than in Nes-GFP+ BMSCs at E18.5.
source: The expression of genes associated with chondrocyte development was higher in Nes-GFP- than in Nes-GFP+ BMSCs at E18.5; in contrast, the expression of master regulators of chondrogenesis, osteogenesis, and adipogenesis was progressively enriched in postnatal Nes-GFP+ BMSCs (Figure 3L), consistent with the increasing MSC enrichment in this population.
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 3L.

claim: The expression of master regulators of chondrogenesis, osteogenesis, and adipogenesis was progressively enriched in postnatal Nes-GFP+ BMSCs.
source: The expression of genes associated with chondrocyte development was higher in Nes-GFP- than in Nes-GFP+ BMSCs at E18.5; in contrast, the expression of master regulators of chondrogenesis, osteogenesis, and adipogenesis was progressively enriched in postnatal Nes-GFP+ BMSCs (Figure 3L), consistent with the increasing MSC enrichment in this population.
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR analysis comparing E18.5 and P7 samples in Figure 3L.

claim: Most fetal BMSCs do not express nestin and quickly differentiate towards committed skeletal precursors, losing most MSC activity by the second week after birth.
source: Together, these results suggest that most fetal BMSCs do not express nestin and quickly differentiate towards committed skeletal precursors, losing most MSC activity by the second week after birth.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of CFU-F assays, gene expression analysis, and differentiation assays shown in Figure 3.

claim: Nestin+ cells conserve MSC activity throughout life.
source: In contrast, nestin+ cells conserve MSC activity throughout life.
evidence: This is demonstrated by CFU-F assays showing maintained activity in Nes-GFP+ cells from fetal to adult stages (Figure 3H).

claim: Limb bones from Wnt1-Cre2;R26-Tomato double-transgenic neonates showed some neural crest-derived osteoblasts and osteocytes aligning the most recent layers of bone deposition.
source: Unexpectedly, limb bones from Wnt1-Cre2;R26-Tomato double-transgenic neonates showed some neural crest-derived osteoblasts and osteocytes aligning the most recent layers of bone deposition, as well as similarly distributed chondrocytes in the outermost layers of the femur head (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fate mapping shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Limb bones from Wnt1-Cre2;R26-Tomato double-transgenic neonates showed neural crest-derived chondrocytes in the outermost layers of the femur head.
source: Unexpectedly, limb bones from Wnt1-Cre2;R26-Tomato double-transgenic neonates showed some neural crest-derived osteoblasts and osteocytes aligning the most recent layers of bone deposition, as well as similarly distributed chondrocytes in the outermost layers of the femur head (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fate mapping shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Neural crest-traced Schwann cells expressing glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) were detected in the bone marrow of one-week old mice.
source: As expected, neural crest-traced Schwann cells expressing glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) were also detected in the bone marrow of one-week old mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: GFAP− perivascular cells with a similar morphology and distribution to Nes-GFP+ cells were derived from Wnt1+ cells.
source: Intriguingly, GFAP− perivascular cells with a similar morphology and distribution to Nes-GFP+ cells were also derived from Wnt1+ cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fate mapping shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: The number of neural crest-traced osteochondral cells increased in the first postnatal week.
source: The number of neural crest-traced osteochondral cells increased in the first postnatal week (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown by quantification of Tomato+ cells in Figure 4C.

claim: By P28, CFU-F activity was much higher in Wnt1-Cre2-traced cells than in non-neural crest-traced bone marrow stromal cells.
source: By P28, CFU-F activity was much higher in Wnt1-Cre2-traced cells than in non-neural crest-traced bone marrow stromal cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CFU-F assays on sorted populations shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The neural crest contributes to limb bones late in development.
source: These results show that the neural crest contributes to limb bones late in development.
evidence: This is inferred from the fate mapping and functional data showing neural crest-derived osteochondral cells appearing postnatally.

claim: Pdgfrα+ BMSCs are highly enriched in CFU-F activity.
source: Mouse Pdgfrα+ BMSCs are highly enriched in CFU-F activity (Takashima et al., 2007; Morikawa et al., 2009a) and most adult mouse bone marrow nestin+ cells are also Pdgfrα+ (Yamazaki et al., 2011; Pinho et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Most adult mouse bone marrow nestin+ cells are Pdgfrα+.
source: Mouse Pdgfrα+ BMSCs are highly enriched in CFU-F activity (Takashima et al., 2007; Morikawa et al., 2009a) and most adult mouse bone marrow nestin+ cells are also Pdgfrα+ (Yamazaki et al., 2011; Pinho et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pdgfrα+ BMSCs were enriched in CFU-F activity at fetal stages.
source: We found that Pdgfrα+ BMSCs were also enriched in CFU-F activity at fetal stages (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CFU-F assays on sorted fetal populations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: In the bone marrow of 4-week old Nes-Gfp;Wnt1-Cre2;R26-Tomato mice, most neural crest-traced cells were Pdgfrα+ and Nes-GFP+.
source: In the bone marrow of 4-week old Nes-Gfp;Wnt1-Cre2;R26-Tomato mice, most neural crest-traced cells were also Pdgfrα+ and Nes-GFP+ (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Most Sox10-CreERT2-traced bone marrow stromal cells were Pdgfrα+ and Nes-GFP+ cells.
source: Similar to the situation in stage-matched Nes-Gfp mice—and also consistent with Wnt1-Cre2-traced cells—most Sox10-CreERT2-traced bone marrow stromal cells were Pdgfrα+ and Nes-GFP+ cells (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The neural crest contributes to nestin+ BMSCs.
source: These results thus demonstrate definitively that the neural crest contributes to nestin+ BMSCs.
evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from multiple lines of fate mapping evidence using Wnt1-Cre2 and Sox10-CreERT2 mice.

claim: Bone marrow Nes-GFP+ cells were closely associated with distinctive Gfap+ Schwann cells.
source: We found that bone marrow Nes-GFP+ cells were closely associated with distinctive Gfap+ Schwann cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The expression levels of HSC maintenance genes (Cxcl12, Kitl and Angpt1) was highly enriched in GFP+ Pdgfrα+ cells.
source: Interestingly, whereas Ly6a/Sca1 expression was higher in GFP−Pdgfrα+ cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B), the expression levels of HSC maintenance genes (Cxcl12, Kitl and Angpt1) and the Leptin receptor, which marks HSC niche-forming mesenchymal cells (Ding et al., 2012), was highly enriched in GFP+ Pdgfrα+ cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The Leptin receptor, which marks HSC niche-forming mesenchymal cells, was highly enriched in GFP+ Pdgfrα+ cells.
source: Interestingly, whereas Ly6a/Sca1 expression was higher in GFP−Pdgfrα+ cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B), the expression levels of HSC maintenance genes (Cxcl12, Kitl and Angpt1) and the Leptin receptor, which marks HSC niche-forming mesenchymal cells (Ding et al., 2012), was highly enriched in GFP+ Pdgfrα+ cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5B and supported by citation.

claim: GFP+ Pdgfrα+ cells abundantly expressed genes enriched in MSCs.
source: This population also abundantly expressed other genes enriched in MSCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Nes-GFP+ Pdgfrα− cells expressed genes characteristic of Schwann cell precursors (Sox10, Plp1, Erbb3, Dhh).
source: In contrast, Nes-GFP+ Pdgfrα− cells expressed genes characteristic of Schwann cell precursors (Sox10, Plp1, Erbb3, Dhh) but did not express mature Schwann cell genes, such as Gfap (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Nes-GFP+ Pdgfrα− cells did not express mature Schwann cell genes, such as Gfap.
source: In contrast, Nes-GFP+ Pdgfrα− cells expressed genes characteristic of Schwann cell precursors (Sox10, Plp1, Erbb3, Dhh) but did not express mature Schwann cell genes, such as Gfap (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Nes-GFP+ Pdgfrα+ cells were more similar to adult primitive BMSCs and distinct from more differentiated osteoblastic cells.
source: Unbiased hierarchical clustering and principal component analysis (Figure 5D) revealed that Nes-GFP+ Pdgfrα+ cells were more similar to adult primitive BMSCs and distinct from more differentiated osteoblastic cells (Nakamura et al., 2010).
evidence: This is demonstrated by principal component analysis shown in Figure 5D and supported by citation.

claim: Nes-GFP+ Pdgfrα− cells' genomic profile was closest to that of E12.5 Schwann cell precursors.
source: In addition, Nes-GFP+ Pdgfrα + cells clustered far from Nes-GFP+ Pdgfrα− cells, whose genomic profile was closest to that of E12.5 Schwann cell precursors.
evidence: This is demonstrated by principal component analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Mesenchymal and glial differentiation was segregated in Pdgfrα+ and Pdgfrα− cells, respectively.
source: To test this hypothesis functionally, we cultured neonatal Nes-GFP+/− Pdgfrα+/− BMSCs in differentiation medium, finding that mesenchymal and glial differentiation was segregated in Pdgfrα+ and Pdgfrα− cells, respectively (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro differentiation assays shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: Two Nes-GFP+ neural crest derivatives occur in postnatal bone marrow: Pdgfrα+ MSCs enriched in HSC-supporting genes and Pdgfrα− Schwann cell precursors.
source: Thus two Nes-GFP+ neural crest derivatives occur in postnatal bone marrow: Pdgfrα+ MSCs enriched in HSC-supporting genes and Pdgfrα− Schwann cell precursors.
evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from the combined transcriptomic and functional characterization of these populations.

claim: Perineural migration of neural crest-derived cells requires the interaction of the receptor tyrosine-protein kinase ErbB3 with the ligand neuregulin-1, produced by developing nerves.
source: Perineural migration of neural crest-derived cells requires the interaction of the receptor tyrosine-protein kinase ErbB3 with the ligand neuregulin-1, produced by developing nerves (Jessen and Mirsky, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Erbb3-deficient mice initially show normal development of peripheral nerves but later display impaired perineural migration of neural crest-derived cells and die at perinatal stage.
source: Erbb3-deficient mice initially show normal development of peripheral nerves but later display impaired perineural migration of neural crest-derived cells and die at perinatal stage (Riethmacher et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Hematopoietic progenitors were increased in fetal liver of Erbb3 KO mice.
source: Hematopoietic progenitors were increased in fetal liver of KO mice (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Expression of the MSC marker CD90 was reduced two-fold in Erbb3−/− limb bone marrow.
source: In contrast, expression of the MSC marker CD90, enriched in Nes-GFP+ cells (Figure 6B,C), was reduced two-fold in Erbb3−/− limb bone marrow, associated with 5-fold drop in the number of bone marrow hematopoietic progenitors (Figure 6D,G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: CD90 is enriched in Nes-GFP+ cells.
source: In contrast, expression of the MSC marker CD90, enriched in Nes-GFP+ cells (Figure 6B,C), was reduced two-fold in Erbb3−/− limb bone marrow, associated with 5-fold drop in the number of bone marrow hematopoietic progenitors (Figure 6D,G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry and immunofluorescence shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: Erbb3−/− limb bone marrow showed a 5-fold drop in the number of bone marrow hematopoietic progenitors.
source: In contrast, expression of the MSC marker CD90, enriched in Nes-GFP+ cells (Figure 6B,C), was reduced two-fold in Erbb3−/− limb bone marrow, associated with 5-fold drop in the number of bone marrow hematopoietic progenitors (Figure 6D,G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 6F-G.

claim: Dhh-Cre;Erbb3fl/fl mice are virtually devoid of Schwann cells.
source: Similar to the constitutive KO, Dhh-Cre;Erbb3fl/fl mice are virtually devoid of Schwann cells (Sheean et al., 2014); however, unlike the constitutive KO, Dhh-Cre;Erbb3fl/fl mice had a normal frequency of bone marrow hematopoietic progenitors (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by citation and demonstrated by flow cytometry in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Dhh-Cre;Erbb3fl/fl mice had a normal frequency of bone marrow hematopoietic progenitors.
source: Similar to the constitutive KO, Dhh-Cre;Erbb3fl/fl mice are virtually devoid of Schwann cells (Sheean et al., 2014); however, unlike the constitutive KO, Dhh-Cre;Erbb3fl/fl mice had a normal frequency of bone marrow hematopoietic progenitors (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Neural crest cells not yet committed to the Schwann cell lineage migrate along developing nerves to the bone marrow, giving rise to HSC niche-forming MSCs.
source: Together, these results suggest that neural crest cells not yet committed to the Schwann cell lineage migrate along developing nerves to the bone marrow, giving rise to HSC niche-forming MSCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of constitutive vs. Schwann cell-specific ErbB3 deletion on bone marrow HSCs.

claim: HSCs show significant proximity to Nes-GFP+ cells in neonatal bone marrow.
source: Despite the low frequency of HSCs and Nes-GFP+ cells, detailed immunofluorescence analysis showed significant proximity of HSCs to Nes-GFP+ cells in neonatal bone marrow (Figure 7A,B), suggesting that nestin+ cells might attract circulating HSCs toward their final developmental destination in the bone marrow.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence imaging and distance quantification shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: Nestin+ cells might attract circulating HSCs toward their final developmental destination in the bone marrow.
source: Despite the low frequency of HSCs and Nes-GFP+ cells, detailed immunofluorescence analysis showed significant proximity of HSCs to Nes-GFP+ cells in neonatal bone marrow (Figure 7A,B), suggesting that nestin+ cells might attract circulating HSCs toward their final developmental destination in the bone marrow.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the spatial proximity data.

claim: Depletion of nestin+ cells at E15.5 in Nes-CreERT2;iDTR mice caused an ∼4-fold reduction in fetal bone marrow HSC activity within 48 hr.
source: Depletion of nestin+ cells at E15.5 in Nes-CreERT2;iDTR mice caused an ∼4-fold reduction in fetal bone marrow HSC activity within 48 hr, inversely correlating with an ∼8-fold increase in fetal liver HSC activity (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LTCIC assays shown in Figure 7C-D.

claim: Depletion of nestin+ cells at E15.5 in Nes-CreERT2;iDTR mice caused an ∼8-fold increase in fetal liver HSC activity.
source: Depletion of nestin+ cells at E15.5 in Nes-CreERT2;iDTR mice caused an ∼4-fold reduction in fetal bone marrow HSC activity within 48 hr, inversely correlating with an ∼8-fold increase in fetal liver HSC activity (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LTCIC assays shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The cell cycle profile and apoptosis in hematopoietic progenitors were unchanged after nestin+ cell depletion.
source: The cell cycle profile and apoptosis in hematopoietic progenitors were unchanged (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), but their numbers increased in fetal liver by 40% (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cell cycle analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Hematopoietic progenitor numbers increased in fetal liver by 40% after nestin+ cell depletion.
source: The cell cycle profile and apoptosis in hematopoietic progenitors were unchanged (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), but their numbers increased in fetal liver by 40% (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry quantification shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Developmental HSC migration to bone marrow proceeds until the second week after birth.
source: Developmental HSC migration to bone marrow proceeds until the second week after birth (Dzierzak and Speck, 2008), suggesting that the bone marrow environment might still mature during this period to accommodate HSCs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and used to interpret the findings.

claim: The expression of HSC-supporting genes was markedly higher and progressively upregulated in GFP+ cells during the first postnatal week.
source: The expression of HSC-supporting genes was markedly higher and progressively upregulated in GFP+ cells during the first postnatal week (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR analysis comparing E18.5 and P7 samples shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Perinatal maturation of nestin+ cells allows the colonization of bone marrow by circulating HSCs.
source: These results suggest that perinatal maturation of nestin+ cells allows the colonization of bone marrow by circulating HSCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal correlation between nestin+ cell maturation and HSC migration.

claim: HSC migration to fetal bone marrow is enhanced by Cxcl12 and stem cell factor.
source: HSC migration to fetal bone marrow is enhanced by Cxcl12 and stem cell factor (Christensen et al., 2004), both of which are highly expressed and progressively upregulated in bone marrow nestin+ cells at perinatal stages (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by citation and demonstrated by qPCR data in Figure 7G.

claim: Cxcl12 and stem cell factor are highly expressed and progressively upregulated in bone marrow nestin+ cells at perinatal stages.
source: HSC migration to fetal bone marrow is enhanced by Cxcl12 and stem cell factor (Christensen et al., 2004), both of which are highly expressed and progressively upregulated in bone marrow nestin+ cells at perinatal stages (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Cxcl12 is produced by several stromal cells and is required for developmental bone marrow colonization by HSCs.
source: Cxcl12 is produced by several stromal cells and is required for developmental bone marrow colonization by HSCs (Ara et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: One week after birth, Cxcl12 mRNA levels in Nes-GFP+ BMSCs were >20-fold higher than in bone marrow endothelial cells.
source: We found that, one week after birth, Cxcl12 mRNA levels in Nes-GFP+ BMSCs were >20-fold higher than in bone marrow endothelial cells and 80-fold higher than in Nes-GFP- BMSCs (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 7H.

claim: One week after birth, Cxcl12 mRNA levels in Nes-GFP+ BMSCs were 80-fold higher than in Nes-GFP- BMSCs.
source: We found that, one week after birth, Cxcl12 mRNA levels in Nes-GFP+ BMSCs were >20-fold higher than in bone marrow endothelial cells and 80-fold higher than in Nes-GFP- BMSCs (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Among neural crest-traced cells, Nes-GFP+ BMSCs were particularly enriched in the expression of Cxcl12 and endogenous Nestin.
source: Among neural crest-traced cells, Nes-GFP+ BMSCs were particularly enriched in the expression of Cxcl12 and endogenous Nestin (Figure 7I,J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR analysis on sorted populations shown in Figure 7I-J.

claim: Nes-CreERT2 mice mostly label Nes-GFP+ cells during the first postnatal week.
source: To conditionally delete Cxcl12 in nestin+ cells in the first postnatal week, we intercrossed Cxcl12 fl mice (Tzeng et al., 2010) with Nes-CreERT2 mice, which mostly label Nes-GFP+ cells during this period (Figure 7K).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fate mapping shown in Figure 7K and supported by citation.

claim: Tamoxifen administration did not significantly alter Cxcl12 mRNA levels in bone marrow endothelial cells in Nes-CreERT2;Cxcl12fl/fl mice.
source: Tamoxifen administration did not significantly alter Cxcl12 mRNA levels in bone marrow endothelial cells but decreased these levels by 5-fold in BMSCs (Figure 7L–M).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 7M.

claim: Tamoxifen administration decreased Cxcl12 mRNA levels by 5-fold in BMSCs in Nes-CreERT2;Cxcl12fl/fl mice.
source: Tamoxifen administration did not significantly alter Cxcl12 mRNA levels in bone marrow endothelial cells but decreased these levels by 5-fold in BMSCs (Figure 7L–M).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 7L.

claim: Deletion of Cxcl12 in nestin+ cells was associated with an ∼30% reduction of bone marrow hematopoietic progenitors.
source: This was associated with an ∼30% reduction of bone marrow hematopoietic progenitors and HSCs measured by long-term competitive repopulation assays (Figure 7N,O).
evidence: This is demonstrated by CFU-C assays shown in Figure 7N.

claim: Deletion of Cxcl12 in nestin+ cells was associated with an ∼30% reduction of bone marrow HSCs measured by long-term competitive repopulation assays.
source: This was associated with an ∼30% reduction of bone marrow hematopoietic progenitors and HSCs measured by long-term competitive repopulation assays (Figure 7N,O).
evidence: This is demonstrated by competitive transplantation assays shown in Figure 7O.

claim: Cxcl12 production by nestin+ MSCs contributes to the HSC niche formation in the developing bone marrow.
source: These results demonstrate that Cxcl12 production by nestin+ MSCs contributes to the HSC niche formation in the developing bone marrow.
evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from the conditional deletion experiments showing impaired HSC migration and maintenance.

claim: The developing bone marrow in axial and appendicular skeleton harbors different MSC populations with distinct origins and specialized roles.
source: We show that the developing bone marrow in axial and appendicular skeleton harbors different MSC populations with distinct origins and specialized roles.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data.

claim: Mesoderm-derived nestin− MSCs give rise to bone and cartilage.
source: While mesoderm-derived nestin− MSCs give rise to bone and cartilage, the neuroectoderm provides an additional source of MSCs, marked by nestin expression, that are endowed with specific HSC niche functions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by lineage tracing and functional assays throughout the manuscript.

claim: The neuroectoderm provides an additional source of MSCs, marked by nestin expression, that are endowed with specific HSC niche functions.
source: While mesoderm-derived nestin− MSCs give rise to bone and cartilage, the neuroectoderm provides an additional source of MSCs, marked by nestin expression, that are endowed with specific HSC niche functions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by neural crest lineage tracing and functional studies throughout the manuscript.

claim: Osteochondroprogenitor and stem cell niche functions are separate and non-overlapping during bone marrow ontogenesis.
source: We therefore conclude that osteochondroprogenitor and stem cell niche functions are separate and non-overlapping during bone marrow ontogenesis.
evidence: This is the central conclusion of the study based on the functional segregation observed.

claim: The neural crest gives rise to three regulators of adult HSC activity: sympathetic neurons, associated Schwann cells, and nestin+ MSCs.
source: The neural crest thus gives rise to three regulators of adult HSC activity: sympathetic neurons, associated Schwann cells, and nestin+ MSCs.
evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from the neural crest lineage tracing studies.

claim: The trunk neural crest is thought to generate mostly non-ectomesenchymal derivatives, including melanocytes, neurons, and glia of the peripheral nervous system.
source: While the neural crest contributes to the craniofacial skeleton, the trunk neural crest is thought to generate mostly non-ectomesenchymal derivatives, including melanocytes, neurons, and glia of the peripheral nervous system.
evidence: This represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: In the trunk skeleton, mesenchymal cells have been considered to be derived mostly from the mesoderm.
source: In the trunk skeleton, mesenchymal cells have thus been considered to be derived mostly from the mesoderm (Olsen et al., 2000), but the neural crest is also a source of pericytes, mural cells, and fibroblasts (Bergwerff et al., 1998; Etchevers et al., 2001; Joseph et al., 2004) that can differentiate into mesenchymal lineages in vitro (Morikawa et al., 2009b; Glejzer et al., 2011; John et al., 2011; Komada et al., 2012).
evidence: This represents established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The neural crest is a source of pericytes, mural cells, and fibroblasts that can differentiate into mesenchymal lineages in vitro.
source: In the trunk skeleton, mesenchymal cells have thus been considered to be derived mostly from the mesoderm (Olsen et al., 2000), but the neural crest is also a source of pericytes, mural cells, and fibroblasts (Bergwerff et al., 1998; Etchevers et al., 2001; Joseph et al., 2004) that can differentiate into mesenchymal lineages in vitro (Morikawa et al., 2009b; Glejzer et al., 2011; John et al., 2011; Komada et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Genetic fate-mapping studies using the neuroepithelial marker Sox1 identified a neuroectodermal origin of the earliest trunk MSCs.
source: Genetic fate-mapping studies using the neuroepithelial marker Sox1 identified a neuroectodermal origin of the earliest trunk MSCs, but other MSCs are recruited from undefined sources at later stages (Takashima et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Other MSCs are recruited from undefined sources at later stages of development.
source: Genetic fate-mapping studies using the neuroepithelial marker Sox1 identified a neuroectodermal origin of the earliest trunk MSCs, but other MSCs are recruited from undefined sources at later stages (Takashima et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents a knowledge gap that the current study addresses.

claim: Osterix-Cre-labeled cells in neonatal bone give rise to Nes-GFP+ MSCs.
source: Very recent data showed that Osterix-Cre-labeled cells in neonatal bone give rise to Nes-GFP+ MSCs (Mizoguchi et al., 2014; Ono et al., 2014); however, the Osterix-Cre lines used in these studies have been shown previously to mark not only osteolineage cells but also a large variety of non-osteolineage cells, including adventitial reticular cells, vascular smooth muscle cells, adipocytes, and perineural cells (Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies and a critical evaluation of the Osterix-Cre line.

claim: The Osterix-Cre lines mark not only osteolineage cells but also a large variety of non-osteolineage cells, including adventitial reticular cells, vascular smooth muscle cells, adipocytes, and perineural cells.
source: Very recent data showed that Osterix-Cre-labeled cells in neonatal bone give rise to Nes-GFP+ MSCs (Mizoguchi et al., 2014; Ono et al., 2014); however, the Osterix-Cre lines used in these studies have been shown previously to mark not only osteolineage cells but also a large variety of non-osteolineage cells, including adventitial reticular cells, vascular smooth muscle cells, adipocytes, and perineural cells (Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Only endochondral cells can form a hematopoietic microenvironment when implanted beneath the kidney capsule.
source: Previous studies suggested that only endochondral cells can form a hematopoietic microenvironment when implanted beneath the kidney capsule (Chan et al., 2008, 2013), although bones formed by intramembranous ossification, such as the skull, can also form hematopoietic marrow without progressing through a cartilage intermediate.
evidence: This is a claim from previous studies that is being discussed and qualified.

claim: Bones formed by intramembranous ossification, such as the skull, can form hematopoietic marrow without progressing through a cartilage intermediate.
source: Previous studies suggested that only endochondral cells can form a hematopoietic microenvironment when implanted beneath the kidney capsule (Chan et al., 2008, 2013), although bones formed by intramembranous ossification, such as the skull, can also form hematopoietic marrow without progressing through a cartilage intermediate.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge that contradicts the previous claim.

claim: CD105 and CD90/Thy1 are particularly enriched in bone marrow Nes-GFP+ cells.
source: Notably, two surface markers used to isolate osteochondrogenic precursors in these studies, CD105 and CD90/Thy1, are particularly enriched in bone marrow Nes-GFP+ cells.
evidence: This is stated based on the authors' observations, though specific data are not shown in the figures.

claim: Neural crest-derived cells that are not yet committed to the Schwann cell lineage migrate to bone in association with developing nerve fibers and give rise to bone marrow nestin+ MSCs with specialized HSC niche functions.
source: Our genetic studies clearly show that neural crest-derived cells that are not yet committed to the Schwann cell lineage migrate to bone in association with developing nerve fibers and give rise to bone marrow nestin+ MSCs with specialized HSC niche functions.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the ErbB3 deletion studies.

claim: Constitutive deletion of the neuregulin-1 receptor ErbB3 reduces BMSC number and impairs developmental HSC migration from liver to bone marrow.
source: Constitutive deletion of the neuregulin-1 receptor ErbB3, which does not directly affect the peripheral nerves but impairs perineural migration of neural crest-derived cells (Riethmacher et al., 1997), reduces BMSC number and impairs developmental HSC migration from liver to bone marrow.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Conditional deletion of ErbB3 in committed glial precursors severely reduced Schwann cell numbers but did not affect bone marrow HSCs.
source: In contrast, conditional deletion of ErbB3 in committed glial precursors severely reduced Schwann cell numbers (Sheean et al., 2014) but did not affect bone marrow HSCs in our study.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and supported by citation.

claim: HSC maintenance genes are highly enriched and progressively upregulated in Nes-GFP+ Pdgfrα+ MSCs, coincident with HSC bone marrow colonization.
source: HSC maintenance genes are highly enriched and progressively upregulated in Nes-GFP+ Pdgfrα+ MSCs, coincident with HSC bone marrow colonization (Christensen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data in Figure 7G and supported by citation.

claim: Perinatal deletion of nestin+ cells prevented HSC bone marrow seeding.
source: Perinatal deletion of nestin+ cells or blockade of their Cxcl12 production prevented HSC bone marrow seeding.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the depletion experiments shown in Figure 7C-F.

claim: Blockade of Cxcl12 production by nestin+ cells prevented HSC bone marrow seeding.
source: Perinatal deletion of nestin+ cells or blockade of their Cxcl12 production prevented HSC bone marrow seeding.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the conditional deletion experiments shown in Figure 7N-O.

claim: Neural crest-derived nestin+ MSCs are required for developmental HSC migration and formation of the bone marrow HSC niche.
source: Therefore, we are confident that neural crest-derived nestin+ MSCs are indeed required for developmental HSC migration and formation of the bone marrow HSC niche.
evidence: This is the authors' conclusion based on all the experimental evidence presented.
